page_header: Cell Cycle and Cell Division · 4 marks

steps.label: Leptotene and zygotene
lines: Prophase I is the longest and most complex stage
of meiosis. It is divided into five sub-stages
according to how the chromosomes behave.

lines.text: Leptotene — the chromosomes become
compact and slowly become visible under the
light microscope.
Zygotene — the homologous chromosomes
pair. This pairing is called synapsis, and a
protein structure called the synaptonemal
complex forms between the paired
chromosomes. A synapsed pair of homologous
chromosomes is called a bivalent or a tetrad.

steps.why: The five sub-stages are each named for one visible change, so the answer is built by taking them in order and stating that change. Leptotene makes the chromosomes visible, zygotene brings the partners together.
common_mistakes: Mixing the order of leptotene and zygotene.
Treating 'synapsis' and 'synaptonemal complex' as the same thing. Synapsis is the pairing; the synaptonemal complex is the protein structure that holds it.
steps.memory_tip: Five sub-stages in order: Leptotene, Zygotene, Pachytene, Diplotene, Diakinesis — L, Z, P, D, D.
steps.margin_note: One line per sub-stage. Do not write a paragraph on any of them.

steps.label: Pachytene

lines.text: Pachytene — the bivalent now clearly shows
four chromatids. Recombination nodules
appear on it, and crossing over takes place at
these points between non-sister chromatids
of the two homologous chromosomes.

steps.why: Pachytene is the sub-stage the examiner marks hardest, because it carries crossing over, and crossing over is the reason meiosis produces variation at all.
common_mistakes: Writing that crossing over happens between sister chromatids.
Placing crossing over in zygotene. Zygotene is only the pairing.
steps.memory_tip: Pachytene is the pairing-plus-exchange stage: four chromatids visible, crossing over happening.
steps.margin_note: Two lines. Name the nodules and say between which chromatids the exchange happens.

steps.label: Labelled diagram
steps.why: A labelled pachytene bivalent shows in one picture what the words take a paragraph to say: two homologues, four chromatids, the synaptonemal complex between the pair, and a chiasma where two non-sister chromatids have exchanged.
common_mistakes: Drawing only two chromatids. A bivalent at pachytene has four.
Leaving the chiasma out. Without it the drawing shows zygotene, not pachytene.
steps.memory_tip: Draw four lines, join each pair at a centromere, put the ladder between the two pairs, and cross the two middle lines once.
steps.margin_note: A simple line drawing with the four labels is enough. Do not shade it or draw a cell around it.

steps.label: Diplotene and diakinesis

lines.text: Diplotene — the synaptonemal complex
dissolves. The homologues move apart except
at the points where they crossed over; those
points are now seen as X-shaped chiasmata.
Diakinesis — the chiasmata move to the ends
of the chromosomes, which is called
terminalisation. The nucleolus and the nuclear
membrane disappear and the spindle forms.
Leptotene → Zygotene → Pachytene → Diplotene → Diakinesis

steps.why: Diplotene reverses the pairing of zygotene, and diakinesis ends prophase I by clearing the nucleus so the spindle can take over. Ending with the ordered list of five names secures the structure mark.
common_mistakes: Writing that the homologues separate completely in diplotene. They stay joined at the chiasmata.
Confusing terminalisation with crossing over. Terminalisation only moves the chiasmata to the ends.
steps.memory_tip: Diplotene shows the chiasmata, diakinesis moves them to the ends.
steps.margin_note: Finish with the ordered list of the five sub-stages, even if you are short of time.

insider_note: Four marks, five sub-stages and one diagram — the answer that scores is a short line for each stage plus the labelled bivalent, not a long paragraph on crossing over.
